I also spiral into worrying about my parents in El Salvador getting sick and me not being able to help, and once these thoughts start, I just can't shut them off.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant life changes or stressors recently that might be contributing to your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion, or have these feelings been more of a gradual development over time?\n\nPatient: It started about seven or eight months ago when I transitioned from my structured college program into a demanding, full-time chemistry lab job. The pressure to prove myself under tight deadlines triggered a gradual spiral of constant worry and exhaustion, and now it's basically become my daily default.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are days when you feel better, or if the feelings of exhaustion and anxiety are constant, and do you think the anxiety is driving the avoidance of activities you used to enjoy, or is it the other way around?\n\nPatient: The exhaustion and anxiety are pretty much constant, and even resting on weekends doesn't help me recover. I'm just so completely drained and wound up that I don't even have the energy to cook or see my friends anymore. It's like the physical exhaustion and tension just take over everything.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned feeling 'wound up' - can you tell me more about what you mean by that, is it like feeling anxious or on edge most of the time?\n\nPatient: Yes, it's like I've had way too much coffee even when I haven't, and I just can't shake that feeling. I'm constantly pacing around the lab, bouncing my leg in meetings, and jumping every time my phone buzzes with a Slack notification. I feel like I'm always bracing for someone to tell me I've made a massive mistake.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific thoughts or worries that are driving your feeling of being 'wound up' and 'bracing for a mistake', or is it more of a general, constant state of tension?\n\nPatient: It’s a mix of both, because my mind is constantly flooded with specific worries like messing up an instrument calibration, ruining data, or causing my PI to lose a grant. I also spiral into worrying about my parents in El Salvador getting sick and me not being able to help, and once these thoughts start, I just can't shut them off.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant life changes or stressors recently that might be contributing to your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion, or have these feelings been more of a gradual development over time?\n\nPatient: It started about seven or eight months ago when I transitioned from my structured college program into a demanding, full-time chemistry lab job. The pressure to prove myself under tight deadlines triggered a gradual spiral of constant worry and exhaustion, and now it's basically become my daily default.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are days when you feel better, or if the feelings of exhaustion and anxiety are constant, and do you think the anxiety is driving the avoidance of activities you used to enjoy, or is it the other way around?\n\nPatient: The exhaustion and anxiety are pretty much constant, and even resting on weekends doesn't help me recover. It is definitely the anxiety and physical drain driving the avoidance, because I feel too mentally keyed up and physically exhausted to paint, hike, or see friends, so I've pulled back from all of it.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific times or situations when your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion seem to significantly worsen or improve, and how do you think this relates to your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities?\n\nPatient: They are at their worst during the workweek, especially when I'm waiting on emails or getting Slack notifications, and they never really improve, even when I try to rest all weekend. Because of this, I'm too physically drained to paint or hike after work, and even if I do try to relax, my mind gets completely hijacked by uncontrollable worries about lab mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense episode of fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, accompanied by symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or feeling like you're going to pass out?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced sudden, intense episodes like that. My anxiety is more of a constant, lingering worry and tension that stays with me throughout the day rather than hitting me in sudden, overwhelming bursts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety affects your daily functioning, specifically in terms of avoidance behaviors and physical symptoms, and do you feel like you're avoiding activities because of fear of having a panic attack or because of the general feeling of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: My productivity at the lab has dropped significantly, and physically, my shoulders are constantly knotted and my jaw aches from clenching. I'm not avoiding activities because of panic attacks, but simply because I feel completely overwhelmed, keyed up, and too physically drained to do anything. By the end of the day, I only have the energy to eat instant noodles and stare at my laptop.\n\nDoctor: You've described a constant state of anxiety and tension without sudden intense episodes, but can you tell me if you've noticed any specific patterns or triggers that consistently make your anxiety worse, such as particular situations, times of day, or social interactions?\n\nPatient: My anxiety definitely spikes with work communication, like hearing a Slack notification or waiting on an email, which instantly makes me worry I've made a mistake. I also feel incredibly tense during meetings or when operating the SEM and XRD instruments in the lab. Ironically, downtime is another major trigger, because as soon as I try to relax or video chat with my family, my mind starts spiraling and replaying past lab errors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities, such as painting and hiking, is primarily due to the physical exhaustion, the anxiety itself, or a combination of both, and how do you think addressing one might impact the other?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a combination of both; the physical exhaustion makes hiking feel impossible because my body feels too heavy and drained, while the constant mental anxiety and racing thoughts intrude on my painting, making it impossible to focus or relax. I feel like they are deeply connected, and if my mind could finally stop worrying all the time, my body probably wouldn't feel so physically worn out.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your new job and adapting to a new life situation, or do you feel like your anxiety has become a more generalized and pervasive part of your daily life, exceeding the boundaries of just coping with work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the stress of the new lab job, but now it has become a generalized and pervasive part of my daily life. The anxiety follows me everywhere, intruding on my painting, hiking, and even video calls with my family. I find myself constantly spiraling over non-work things too, like my family's health in El Salvador and paying rent, even when I'm just trying to relax at home.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that you don't feel hopeless or depressed, but you've stopped doing things you enjoy due to feeling drained and anxious; can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it's fleeting, or if everything feels empty and unrewarding to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how to answer that, but it feels less like things are completely empty. It's more that I am just too exhausted, and my mind is so crowded with constant worries that I can't actually focus on or enjoy anything anymore.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any recent instances, no matter how small, where you felt a genuine sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it was just for a moment?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it has been incredibly difficult to experience any real enjoyment lately because I'm usually too exhausted to even attempt hobbies I used to love, like painting, hiking, or cooking. Even on the rare occasions I try to relax, like watching a game or video chatting with my family, my mind quickly gets hijacked by intrusive worries about lab mistakes. That constant mental intrusion completely prevents me from feeling any genuine pleasure.\n\nDoctor: You've described a significant impact of your anxiety and exhaustion on your daily life and activities, but can you tell me if you feel like your symptoms are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your job and life changes, or if they seem to be a more intrinsic part of your emotional state?"

Instead, it is more about the constant, overwhelming worry of making mistakes and letting people down, combined with sheer exhaustion.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are primarily a reaction to the stress of your new job and life situation, or have they become a more persistent and pervasive part of your daily life, affecting areas beyond just work-related stress?"

Ironically, downtime is another major trigger, because as soon as I try to relax or video chat with my family, my mind starts spiraling and replaying past lab errors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities, such as painting and hiking, is primarily due to the physical exhaustion, the anxiety itself, or a combination of both, and how do you think addressing one might impact the other?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a combination of both; the physical exhaustion makes hiking feel impossible because my body feels too heavy and drained, while the constant mental anxiety and racing thoughts intrude on my painting, making it impossible to focus or relax. I feel like they are deeply connected, and if my mind could finally stop worrying all the time, my body probably wouldn't feel so physically worn out.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your new job and adapting to a new life situation, or do you feel like your anxiety has become a more generalized and pervasive part of your daily life, exceeding the boundaries of just coping with work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the stress of the new lab job, but now it has become a generalized and pervasive part of my daily life. I find myself constantly spiraling over non-work things too, like my family's health in El Salvador and paying rent, even when I'm just trying to relax at home.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that you don't feel hopeless or depressed, but you've stopped doing things you enjoy due to feeling drained and anxious; can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it's fleeting, or if everything feels empty and unrewarding to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how to answer that, but it feels less like things are completely empty. It's more that I am just too exhausted, and my mind is so crowded with constant worries that I can't actually focus on or enjoy anything anymore.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any recent instances, no matter how small, where you felt a genuine sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it was just for a moment?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it has been incredibly difficult to experience any real enjoyment lately because I'm usually too exhausted to even attempt hobbies I used to love, like painting, hiking, or cooking. Even on the rare occasions I try to relax, like watching a game or video chatting with my family, my mind quickly gets hijacked by intrusive worries about lab mistakes. That constant mental intrusion completely prevents me from feeling any genuine pleasure.\n\nDoctor: You've described a significant impact of your anxiety and exhaustion on your daily life and activities, but can you tell me if you feel like your symptoms are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your job and life changes, or if they seem to be a more intrinsic part of your emotional state?\n\nPatient: While these feelings definitely intensified when I transitioned to this demanding lab job seven or eight months ago, it now feels like a constant, intrinsic state of mind. Instead, it is more about the constant, overwhelming worry of making mistakes and letting people down, combined with sheer exhaustion.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are primarily a reaction to the stress of your new job and life situation, or have they become a more persistent and pervasive part of your daily life, affecting areas beyond just work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the transition to my new lab job seven or eight months ago, but it has become a persistent, everyday struggle that goes far beyond just work. The anxiety and exhaustion now spill over into my personal life, preventing me from enjoying painting, hiking, cooking, or even talking to my family without being consumed by worry.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities would significantly improve if your work situation or other external stressors were to change, or do you feel like your anxiety has taken on a life of its own and would persist regardless of changes in your external circumstances?\n\nPatient: I’m not entirely sure since I haven't had a break from this job to really find out. I'm just so completely drained and wound up that I don't even have the energy to cook or see my friends anymore. It's like the physical exhaustion and tension just take over everything.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned feeling 'wound up' - can you tell me more about what you mean by that, is it like feeling anxious or on edge most of the time?\n\nPatient: Yes, it's like I've had way too much coffee even when I haven't, and I just can't shake that feeling. I'm constantly pacing around the lab, bouncing my leg in meetings, and jumping every time my phone buzzes with a Slack notification. I feel like I'm always bracing for someone to tell me I've made a massive mistake.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific thoughts or worries that are driving your feeling of being 'wound up' and 'bracing for a mistake', or is it more of a general, constant state of tension?\n\nPatient: It’s a mix of both, because my mind is constantly flooded with specific worries like messing up an instrument calibration, ruining data, or causing my PI to lose a grant. I also spiral into worrying about my parents in El Salvador getting sick and me not being able to help, and once these thoughts start, I just can't shut them off.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant life changes or stressors recently that might be contributing to your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion, or have these feelings been more of a gradual development over time?\n\nPatient: It started about seven or eight months ago when I transitioned from my structured college program into a demanding, full-time chemistry lab job. The pressure to prove myself under tight deadlines triggered a gradual spiral of constant worry and exhaustion, and now it's basically become my daily default.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are days when you feel better, or if the feelings of exhaustion and anxiety are constant, and do you think the anxiety is driving the avoidance of activities you used to enjoy, or is it the other way around?\n\nPatient: The exhaustion and anxiety are pretty much constant, and even resting on weekends doesn't help me recover. It is definitely the anxiety and physical drain driving the avoidance, because I feel too mentally keyed up and physically exhausted to paint, hike, or see friends, so I've pulled back from all of it.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific times or situations when your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion seem to significantly worsen or improve, and how do you think this relates to your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities?\n\nPatient: They are at their worst during the workweek, especially when I'm waiting on emails or getting Slack notifications, and they never really improve, even when I try to rest all weekend. Because of this, I'm too physically drained to paint or hike after work, and even if I do try to relax, my mind gets completely hijacked by uncontrollable worries about lab mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense episode of fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, accompanied by symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or feeling like you're going to pass out?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced sudden, intense episodes like that. My anxiety is more of a constant, lingering worry and tension that stays with me throughout the day rather than hitting me in sudden, overwhelming bursts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety affects your daily functioning, specifically in terms of avoidance behaviors and physical symptoms, and do you feel like you're avoiding activities because of fear of having a panic attack or because of the general feeling of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: My productivity at the lab has dropped significantly, and physically, my shoulders are constantly knotted and my jaw aches from clenching. I'm not avoiding activities because of panic attacks, but simply because I feel completely overwhelmed, keyed up, and too physically drained to do anything. By the end of the day, I only have the energy to eat instant noodles and stare at my laptop.\n\nDoctor: You've described a constant state of anxiety and tension without sudden intense episodes, but can you tell me if you've noticed any specific patterns or triggers that consistently make your anxiety worse, such as particular situations, times of day, or social interactions?\n\nPatient: My anxiety definitely spikes with work communication, like hearing a Slack notification or waiting on an email, which instantly makes me worry I've made a mistake. I also feel incredibly tense during meetings or when operating the SEM and XRD instruments in the lab. Ironically, downtime is another major trigger, because as soon as I try to relax or video chat with my family, my mind starts spiraling and replaying past lab errors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities, such as painting and hiking, is primarily due to the physical exhaustion, the anxiety itself, or a combination of both, and how do you think addressing one might impact the other?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a combination of both; the physical exhaustion makes hiking feel impossible because my body feels too heavy and drained, while the constant mental anxiety and racing thoughts intrude on my painting, making it impossible to focus or relax. I feel like they are deeply connected, and if my mind could finally stop worrying all the time, my body probably wouldn't feel so physically worn out.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your new job and adapting to a new life situation, or do you feel like your anxiety has become a more generalized and pervasive part of your daily life, exceeding the boundaries of just coping with work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the stress of the new lab job, but now it has become a generalized and pervasive part of my daily life. The anxiety follows me everywhere, intruding on my painting, hiking, and even video calls with my family. I find myself constantly spiraling over non-work things too, like my family's health in El Salvador and paying rent, even when I'm just trying to relax at home.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that you don't feel hopeless or depressed, but you've stopped doing things you enjoy due to feeling drained and anxious; can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it's fleeting, or if everything feels empty and unrewarding to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how to answer that, but it feels less like things are completely empty. It's more that I am just too exhausted, and my mind is so crowded with constant worries that I can't actually focus on or enjoy anything anymore.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any recent instances, no matter how small, where you felt a genuine sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it was just for a moment?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it has been incredibly difficult to experience any real enjoyment lately because I'm usually too exhausted to even attempt hobbies I used to love, like painting, hiking, or cooking. Even on the rare occasions I try to relax, like watching a game or video chatting with my family, my mind quickly gets hijacked by intrusive worries about lab mistakes. That constant mental intrusion completely prevents me from feeling any genuine pleasure.\n\nDoctor: You've described a significant impact of your anxiety and exhaustion on your daily life and activities, but can you tell me if you feel like your symptoms are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your job and life changes, or if they seem to be a more intrinsic part of your emotional state?\n\nPatient: While these feelings definitely intensified when I transitioned to this demanding lab job seven or eight months ago, it now feels like a constant, intrinsic state of mind. Even though work triggered it, the anxiety has spiraled to the point where my brain is constantly running and worrying about everything, from my family back home to minor daily details. It has basically become my default setting that I just can't seem to shut off anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are more about fearing specific outcomes or consequences related to your job or life, or are they more about the emotional distress and impairment in your daily functioning caused by the constant state of anxiety itself?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both. I’m deeply terrified of specific worst-case scenarios, like ruining a calibration, causing my PI to lose a grant, getting fired, or not being able to support my family in El Salvador. But at the same time, the constant physical exhaustion and tension—and being too drained to paint, hike, or even cook—has become a massive source of distress and impairment on its own.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any periods where your low energy and avoidance of activities are accompanied by feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or self-criticism, or if these feelings are largely absent?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about it that way, and those specific feelings of worthlessness or guilt aren't really what I am experiencing. Instead, it is more about the constant, overwhelming worry of making mistakes and letting people down, combined with sheer exhaustion.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are primarily a reaction to the stress of your new job and life situation, or have they become a more persistent and pervasive part of your daily life, affecting areas beyond just work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the transition to my new lab job seven or eight months ago, but it has become a persistent, everyday struggle that goes far beyond just work. The anxiety and exhaustion now spill over into my personal life, preventing me from enjoying painting, hiking, cooking, or even talking to my family without being consumed by worry.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities would significantly improve if your work situation or other external stressors were to change, or do you feel like your anxiety has taken on a life of its own and would persist regardless of changes in your external circumstances?\n\nPatient: I’m not entirely sure since I haven't had a break from this job to really find out. But right now, it definitely feels like the worry has taken on a mind of its own and is incredibly hard to shut off, even when I'm completely away from the lab.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of relief or calmness after avoiding or escaping from a situation that triggers your anxiety, or if the anxiety persists even after you've removed yourself from the stressful situation?\n\nPatient: The anxiety definitely persists even when I'm completely away from the lab. Even when I'm at home on the weekend trying to relax, watch a game, or rest, I just can't shut the worrying thoughts off. Instead of finding relief, I still feel completely keyed up and physically exhausted.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are more related to a persistent and excessive worry about everyday things, or are they primarily a reaction to the significant life change of starting your new lab job?"

It has definitely become a persistent and excessive worry about almost everything in my life.

It is definitely the anxiety and physical drain driving the avoidance, because I feel too mentally keyed up and physically exhausted to paint, hike, or see friends, so I've pulled back from all of it.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific times or situations when your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion seem to significantly worsen or improve, and how do you think this relates to your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities?\n\nPatient: They are at their worst during the workweek, especially when I'm waiting on emails or getting Slack notifications, and they never really improve, even when I try to rest all weekend. Because of this, I'm too physically drained to paint or hike after work, and even if I do try to relax, my mind gets completely hijacked by uncontrollable worries about lab mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense episode of fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, accompanied by symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or feeling like you're going to pass out?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced sudden, intense episodes like that. My anxiety is more of a constant, lingering worry and tension that stays with me throughout the day rather than hitting me in sudden, overwhelming bursts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety affects your daily functioning, specifically in terms of avoidance behaviors and physical symptoms, and do you feel like you're avoiding activities because of fear of having a panic attack or because of the general feeling of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: My productivity at the lab has dropped significantly, and physically, my shoulders are constantly knotted and my jaw aches from clenching. I'm not avoiding activities because of panic attacks, but simply because I feel completely overwhelmed, keyed up, and too physically drained to do anything. By the end of the day, I only have the energy to eat instant noodles and stare at my laptop.\n\nDoctor: You've described a constant state of anxiety and tension without sudden intense episodes, but can you tell me if you've noticed any specific patterns or triggers that consistently make your anxiety worse, such as particular situations, times of day, or social interactions?\n\nPatient: My anxiety definitely spikes with work communication, like hearing a Slack notification or waiting on an email, which instantly makes me worry I've made a mistake. I also feel incredibly tense during meetings or when operating the SEM and XRD instruments in the lab. Ironically, downtime is another major trigger, because as soon as I try to relax or video chat with my family, my mind starts spiraling and replaying past lab errors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities, such as painting and hiking, is primarily due to the physical exhaustion, the anxiety itself, or a combination of both, and how do you think addressing one might impact the other?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a combination of both; the physical exhaustion makes hiking feel impossible because my body feels too heavy and drained, while the constant mental anxiety and racing thoughts intrude on my painting, making it impossible to focus or relax. I feel like they are deeply connected, and if my mind could finally stop worrying all the time, my body probably wouldn't feel so physically worn out.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your new job and adapting to a new life situation, or do you feel like your anxiety has become a more generalized and pervasive part of your daily life, exceeding the boundaries of just coping with work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the stress of the new lab job, but now it has become a generalized and pervasive part of my daily life. The anxiety follows me everywhere, intruding on my painting, hiking, and even video calls with my family. I find myself constantly spiraling over non-work things too, like my family's health in El Salvador and paying rent, even when I'm just trying to relax at home.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that you don't feel hopeless or depressed, but you've stopped doing things you enjoy due to feeling drained and anxious; can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it's fleeting, or if everything feels empty and unrewarding to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how to answer that, but it feels less like things are completely empty. Even though work triggered it, the anxiety has spiraled to the point where my brain is constantly running and worrying about everything, from my family back home to minor daily details. It has basically become my default setting that I just can't seem to shut off anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are more about fearing specific outcomes or consequences related to your job or life, or are they more about the emotional distress and impairment in your daily functioning caused by the constant state of anxiety itself?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both. The anxiety and exhaustion now spill over into my personal life, preventing me from enjoying painting, hiking, cooking, or even talking to my family without being consumed by worry.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities would significantly improve if your work situation or other external stressors were to change, or do you feel like your anxiety has taken on a life of its own and would persist regardless of changes in your external circumstances?\n\nPatient: I’m not entirely sure since I haven't had a break from this job to really find out. But right now, it definitely feels like the worry has taken on a mind of its own and is incredibly hard to shut off, even when I'm completely away from the lab.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of relief or calmness after avoiding or escaping from a situation that triggers your anxiety, or if the anxiety persists even after you've removed yourself from the stressful situation?\n\nPatient: The anxiety definitely persists even when I'm completely away from the lab. Even when I'm at home on the weekend trying to relax, watch a game, or rest, I just can't shut the worrying thoughts off. It's like the physical exhaustion and tension just take over everything.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned feeling 'wound up' - can you tell me more about what you mean by that, is it like feeling anxious or on edge most of the time?\n\nPatient: Yes, it's like I've had way too much coffee even when I haven't, and I just can't shake that feeling. I'm constantly pacing around the lab, bouncing my leg in meetings, and jumping every time my phone buzzes with a Slack notification. I feel like I'm always bracing for someone to tell me I've made a massive mistake.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific thoughts or worries that are driving your feeling of being 'wound up' and 'bracing for a mistake', or is it more of a general, constant state of tension?\n\nPatient: It’s a mix of both, because my mind is constantly flooded with specific worries like messing up an instrument calibration, ruining data, or causing my PI to lose a grant. I also spiral into worrying about my parents in El Salvador getting sick and me not being able to help, and once these thoughts start, I just can't shut them off.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant life changes or stressors recently that might be contributing to your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion, or have these feelings been more of a gradual development over time?\n\nPatient: It started about seven or eight months ago when I transitioned from my structured college program into a demanding, full-time chemistry lab job. The pressure to prove myself under tight deadlines triggered a gradual spiral of constant worry and exhaustion, and now it's basically become my daily default.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are days when you feel better, or if the feelings of exhaustion and anxiety are constant, and do you think the anxiety is driving the avoidance of activities you used to enjoy, or is it the other way around?\n\nPatient: The exhaustion and anxiety are pretty much constant, and even resting on weekends doesn't help me recover. It is definitely the anxiety and physical drain driving the avoidance, because I feel too mentally keyed up and physically exhausted to paint, hike, or see friends, so I've pulled back from all of it.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any specific times or situations when your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion seem to significantly worsen or improve, and how do you think this relates to your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities?\n\nPatient: They are at their worst during the workweek, especially when I'm waiting on emails or getting Slack notifications, and they never really improve, even when I try to rest all weekend. Because of this, I'm too physically drained to paint or hike after work, and even if I do try to relax, my mind gets completely hijacked by uncontrollable worries about lab mistakes.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a sudden, intense episode of fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, accompanied by symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or feeling like you're going to pass out?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced sudden, intense episodes like that. My anxiety is more of a constant, lingering worry and tension that stays with me throughout the day rather than hitting me in sudden, overwhelming bursts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your anxiety affects your daily functioning, specifically in terms of avoidance behaviors and physical symptoms, and do you feel like you're avoiding activities because of fear of having a panic attack or because of the general feeling of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: My productivity at the lab has dropped significantly, and physically, my shoulders are constantly knotted and my jaw aches from clenching. I'm not avoiding activities because of panic attacks, but simply because I feel completely overwhelmed, keyed up, and too physically drained to do anything. By the end of the day, I only have the energy to eat instant noodles and stare at my laptop.\n\nDoctor: You've described a constant state of anxiety and tension without sudden intense episodes, but can you tell me if you've noticed any specific patterns or triggers that consistently make your anxiety worse, such as particular situations, times of day, or social interactions?\n\nPatient: My anxiety definitely spikes with work communication, like hearing a Slack notification or waiting on an email, which instantly makes me worry I've made a mistake. I also feel incredibly tense during meetings or when operating the SEM and XRD instruments in the lab. Ironically, downtime is another major trigger, because as soon as I try to relax or video chat with my family, my mind starts spiraling and replaying past lab errors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your avoidance of previously enjoyed activities, such as painting and hiking, is primarily due to the physical exhaustion, the anxiety itself, or a combination of both, and how do you think addressing one might impact the other?\n\nPatient: It is definitely a combination of both; the physical exhaustion makes hiking feel impossible because my body feels too heavy and drained, while the constant mental anxiety and racing thoughts intrude on my painting, making it impossible to focus or relax. I feel like they are deeply connected, and if my mind could finally stop worrying all the time, my body probably wouldn't feel so physically worn out.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your new job and adapting to a new life situation, or do you feel like your anxiety has become a more generalized and pervasive part of your daily life, exceeding the boundaries of just coping with work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the stress of the new lab job, but now it has become a generalized and pervasive part of my daily life. The anxiety follows me everywhere, intruding on my painting, hiking, and even video calls with my family. I find myself constantly spiraling over non-work things too, like my family's health in El Salvador and paying rent, even when I'm just trying to relax at home.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that you don't feel hopeless or depressed, but you've stopped doing things you enjoy due to feeling drained and anxious; can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it's fleeting, or if everything feels empty and unrewarding to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how to answer that, but it feels less like things are completely empty. It's more that I am just too exhausted, and my mind is so crowded with constant worries that I can't actually focus on or enjoy anything anymore.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any recent instances, no matter how small, where you felt a genuine sense of pleasure or enjoyment, even if it was just for a moment?\n\nPatient: Honestly, it has been incredibly difficult to experience any real enjoyment lately because I'm usually too exhausted to even attempt hobbies I used to love, like painting, hiking, or cooking. Even on the rare occasions I try to relax, like watching a game or video chatting with my family, my mind quickly gets hijacked by intrusive worries about lab mistakes. That constant mental intrusion completely prevents me from feeling any genuine pleasure.\n\nDoctor: You've described a significant impact of your anxiety and exhaustion on your daily life and activities, but can you tell me if you feel like your symptoms are primarily in response to the specific stressors of your job and life changes, or if they seem to be a more intrinsic part of your emotional state?\n\nPatient: While these feelings definitely intensified when I transitioned to this demanding lab job seven or eight months ago, it now feels like a constant, intrinsic state of mind. Even though work triggered it, the anxiety has spiraled to the point where my brain is constantly running and worrying about everything, from my family back home to minor daily details. It has basically become my default setting that I just can't seem to shut off anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are more about fearing specific outcomes or consequences related to your job or life, or are they more about the emotional distress and impairment in your daily functioning caused by the constant state of anxiety itself?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both. I’m deeply terrified of specific worst-case scenarios, like ruining a calibration, causing my PI to lose a grant, getting fired, or not being able to support my family in El Salvador. But at the same time, the constant physical exhaustion and tension—and being too drained to paint, hike, or even cook—has become a massive source of distress and impairment on its own.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any periods where your low energy and avoidance of activities are accompanied by feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or self-criticism, or if these feelings are largely absent?\n\nPatient: I haven't really thought about it that way, and those specific feelings of worthlessness or guilt aren't really what I am experiencing. Instead, it is more about the constant, overwhelming worry of making mistakes and letting people down, combined with sheer exhaustion.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are primarily a reaction to the stress of your new job and life situation, or have they become a more persistent and pervasive part of your daily life, affecting areas beyond just work-related stress?\n\nPatient: It definitely started with the transition to my new lab job seven or eight months ago, but it has become a persistent, everyday struggle that goes far beyond just work. The anxiety and exhaustion now spill over into my personal life, preventing me from enjoying painting, hiking, cooking, or even talking to my family without being consumed by worry.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you feel like your anxiety and avoidance of activities would significantly improve if your work situation or other external stressors were to change, or do you feel like your anxiety has taken on a life of its own and would persist regardless of changes in your external circumstances?\n\nPatient: I’m not entirely sure since I haven't had a break from this job to really find out. But right now, it definitely feels like the worry has taken on a mind of its own and is incredibly hard to shut off, even when I'm completely away from the lab.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel a sense of relief or calmness after avoiding or escaping from a situation that triggers your anxiety, or if the anxiety persists even after you've removed yourself from the stressful situation?\n\nPatient: The anxiety definitely persists even when I'm completely away from the lab. Even when I'm at home on the weekend trying to relax, watch a game, or rest, I just can't shut the worrying thoughts off. Instead of finding relief, I still feel completely keyed up and physically exhausted.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety and avoidance behaviors are more related to a persistent and excessive worry about everyday things, or are they primarily a reaction to the significant life change of starting your new lab job?\n\nPatient: While starting the lab job seven or eight months ago definitely triggered everything, it now feels like a constant, uncontrollable state that goes far beyond work. I find myself excessively worrying about everyday things like my parents' health in El Salvador, paying rent, or even a delayed email response, which quickly spirals into feeling like my whole life is falling apart. It has definitely become a persistent and excessive worry about almost everything in my life.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced significant physical symptoms like headaches, muscle tension, or sleep disturbances alongside your feelings of anxiety and exhaustion, and how often these physical symptoms occur?\n\nPatient: I don't really get headaches, but I experience severe muscle tension almost every day, especially in my shoulders and neck which feel so tight it's like I've been shrugging for hours, and my jaw constantly aches from clenching. I also feel physically wound up and exhausted all the time, waking up feeling like I pulled an all-nighter in the lab even when I crash for ten hours on the weekend.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any activities or things that used to bring you pleasure or relaxation, but now feel empty or unrewarding due to your current state of anxiety and exhaustion?\n\nPatient: Yes, things like painting, hiking, cooking, and my weekend chemistry teaching used to bring me so much relaxation and joy, but now they feel completely out of reach.
